Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Aug 26, 11:13 am, "Reyda !" <rey...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I just want to ask : why oh why would anyone reasonable want to change
> a rule that is already very interesting as it is, which makes quit
> perfect sense in terms of game mechanism, and has yet to see any
> abuse?

"Abuse" isn't the appropriate term. "Overly harsh penalty for what is
essentially a completely random happenstance" is more appropriate.

Contestation, at this point in the history of the game, when there are
1300+ unique vampires that can show up in any deck, is incredibly
random. You can't avoid being in a situation where contestation can be
an issue. You can't plan around it (other than by not using unique
minions in your crypt, which isn't really available enough an option
to even consider in the argument), you can't prepare for it. It is
completely random. And often when it comes up, you just lose the game
outright (I put 10 pool on my first 11 cap minion. My prey then brings
out the exact same minion by pure chance. We both are likely
completely screwed). It is kind of like if a rule was introduced to
the game where at the start of the game, each player turned over their
top card. If any players turned over the same card, they each lose 15
pool. Incredibly unlikely to come up. Not something you can plan to
avoid. Totally debilitating when it happens.

> Why change a fundamental things like retro transfers, governing
> down etc now 15 years after the game's creation ? Is there some
> creativity problem ?

No. It has always been overly harsh. And no one is suggesting doing
away with contestation. Just making it less of a harsh and arbitrary
punishment for showing up.

Examples of things that have been suggested:

- When you yield a contested card, move all the blood from that card
to your pool. This is my current favorite fix, as it is simple and
laser guided. And mostly helps early game, not as much late game.

- You may burn a minion in your uncontrolled region if bringing it
into play would contest a minion in play. Move all blood on that
minion to your pool. Maybe draw a new crypt card. May or may not come
attached to "you may no longer use 2 transfers to move a blood from an
uncontrolled minion to your pool". This, or some version of it, is
what LSJ seems to favor. Totally reasonable in a design sense, but a
lot of folks object to changing the untransfer rule.

- Players alternate control of the contested minion in some fashion,
either by uncontrolling the first one when the second comes into play,
or by flipping them over during untap. This has a lot of fun,
thematically appropriate reasons to recommend it, but also probably
'causes a lot of rules problems. So unlikely to actually go anywhere.

-Peter

My original proposal was one of the latter, and I agree that it is
probably too complicated to implement. For a while I was in favor of
the 'modified transfer' proposals (not represented above - this is
where you are allowed to transfer off of contested minions and/or
transfer more quickly off of minions that could contest).

I'm sympathetic to the former two solutions above (pool dumping
solutions), but while they do reduce the penalty for contesting,
neither they nor the modified transfer rules really help out contested
star decks, which are counting on being able to use the star. It
seems worthwhile to me to make star decks more viable - they're
generally pretty tenuous right now, but seem worth promoting, as they
are a great way of increasing deck diversity, as there are so many
vampires with unique specials around which to base decks. (Ban Pentex
Subversion.) If you're trying to mitigate contesting effects (as
henrik suggests) in the deck design phase, well, you're writing off
star decks altogether.

So, I find myself returning to the 'alternating control' solutions. I
kind of liked Damnans' proposal (infernal contesting!). I think I
also remember someone suggesting a rule whereby each time you paid to
contest in your untap, your copy of the vampire flips face up and all
others flip face down, which seems like a pretty simple way to
alternate control. (That wasn't your original suggestion, was it,
Peter? I should probably look it up, but there's so much to wade
through...) I'd probably combine either with the ability to recoup
some or all blood on the vampire when yielding a contest.

Hope that helps,
Alex

gets control of the vampire until another Methusaleh influences their
copy to full, and the existing copy gets set back to its owner's
uncontrolled region, like Banishment. No contest need be paid.

For example, if your prey gets Arika first, you could wait until
Arika's spent two blood before bringing out your version and banishing
your prey's. Then your prey has to spend two more pool in the
influence phase to control her and banish your copy. Better yet, hope
that somebody rushes her and does some damage. Even if both Arika's
are full, control would pass back and forth, with each Deflection they
play essentially being paid from pool. Table placement of the
contested vamps, possibilities to rush and deplete contestable
vampires, and the contested vampire's reactive abilities become very
important.

This type of contest fits in well with the flavor of the game -
vampires ask "what have you done for me lately?" If they get too
injured or depleted in the service of one Methusaleh, they switch over
to the Methusaleh who's giving them all the resources they need.

It was done in the first part of this entire discussion.

This is my analysis of a vampire contestation.

First part of the analysis is "how many turns do you take to influence
a vampire into play?"

We can all agree that the larger the vampire that the longer it takes
to get into play. It will either take 1, 2, 3 or 4 turns of transfers
to put a vampire into play. Now in addition to taking turns to put
into play, you are also investing pool between the amount of 1 to 11
pool on your vampire.

When you contest a vampire that vampire is turned face down and
removed from play. You must pay 1 pool to contest a vampire or that
vampire is burned.

So if you contest your first vampire you will effectively start the
game with 30 - minus the capacity of the vampire you are contesting.
So until you win the contestation, you effectively can start the game
with as little as 19 pool (if the contested vampire was an 11 cap).
If you lose the contestation then you actually start the game with as
little as 19 pool.

It will take several turns to get your next vampire into play. So
regardless of whether you win or lose the contestation, then it will
take several more turns for you to get your second vampire into play.
So you are looking at taking your first action on turn 6 or 7. If
most games only last 12 to 14 turns then you you have spent the first
half of the game doing nothing. You have lost out on the chance to
participate in any meaningful way for 50% of the game because your
first vampire was contested.

If you had the choice to not contest your first vampire after you saw
another player put the same vampire into play and you chose to begin
influencing another vampire into play instead of forcing the contest,
then you have all the pool on that vampire until you can get it off.
This can be as much as 10 pool. You still don't have a vampire in
play, but you have 10 pool that is inaccessible until you influence it
back off. So you effectivly start the game with 20 pool in the worst
case scenario. You now begin to influence your second vampire. You
are defenseless until you get your second vampire into play. You have
still lost all those turns of playing to again get your first turn 6
or 7. If most games only last 12 to 14 turns then you you have spent
the first half of the game doing nothing. You have lost out on the
chance to participate in any meaningful way for 50% of the game
because you chose not to contest your first vampire. There is no
reasonable way to get your 10 pool back off your vampire and still be
able to particpate in the game at all. The current remedy of
transferring back the 10 pool means that you will spend the next 5
turns transferring back the pool while still not having a vampire in
play to interact with the game. So now you will spend your first 8 or
9 turns just to get your pool onto a vampire who is brought into play
by another player then transferring the pool back off. You will
still need to influence another vampire into play. This will take a
few more turns so by turn 10 or 11 you have your first vampire into
play. The game is almost over at that point in time and you have done
little or no playing of the game.

Once contesting a vampire starts, you effectively lose 1 pool and 1
action from that vampire for every turn that you contest. So in
addition to losing the pool and turns spent influencing that vampire
into play which can be as many as 4 turns and 11 pool, you are not
losing another turn to act and another pool. So on the first turn
that you pay to contest, you have lost 12 pool. On the second turn
that you pay to contest, you have lost 13 pool and so on. Now you
have remember that you started with 30 pool. so by your second turn
contesting you are at 17 pool less the amount that you have influenced
onto your second vampire.

There is no rule based remedy to contesting vampires other than on
person loses all the pool invested on the vampire and all the pool
spent contesting and all the turns spent contesting while the other
player, who won the contest, merely loses all the pool spent
contesting and all the turns spent contesting.

With 1308 vampire in the game and the average crypt containing 12
vampire, the occurrence of contesting a vampire is rare in the
extreme.

There is one card based remedy to contesting vampires, Praxis
Solomon. No other card in the game remedies the situation of
contesting. There are a few other cards in game that modify how much
you pay or who pays, but only one stops the contestation from
continuing, Praxis Solomon. The occurence of contesting a vampire is
rare in the extreme, so there is no reason for a player to include
Praxis: Solomon in their deck. Even if a player did include Praxis:
Solomon in their deck, they would have to draw it, play it without
being blocked, and then get it to pass, it still doesn't alleviate the
loss of pool or turns that is involved with contesting.

Since you lose the capacity in pool, the turns spent influencing, the
turns spent contesting, pool spent to contest, and there is no rule-
based remedy to this, this disproportionately increases the cost of
contesting the larger the capacity of the vampire is.

In chess it is at least theoretically a viable strategy to look at the
pieces on the board and, if there is one, figure out the game plan
that guarantees a 100% certain win. In V:TES nearly every play has
some chance to backfire or be ineffective. This means that a V:TES
player can only viably plan a certain number of moves ahead before the
risks involved stack up too high. Therefore the V:TES player is to
some extent forced to rely on a good strategy and make moves that
improve his overall position, whereas the chess player only has to
rely on the particular tactic that will guarantee the win.

And that is the value luck has for me in this game.

I don't see the circularity. There used to be a time when there were

random sort -- was therefore less rare, and "pure-luck" variety
contestation therefore had more impact than it does now.

an impact. There is value, in gaming, in obliging players to cope
with the unexpected.

But if rarity implies minimal impact, perhaps we should introduce card-
based mechanisms into the game that make contesting less unlikely,
despite the vast number of vampires. For instance, cards that steal
vampires (with no blood) from another methuselahs uncontrolled region.

The current rules have some potential to be decisive, but there may
also be considerable potential for coping. I cannot see that they are

No strawman. I was describing my own thoughts, not yours. A higher
level of rarity of a random event DOES tend to imply a smaller level
of impact on the game as a whole. I had mentioned this this earlier
in the post, and was carrying the thought forward.

> Randomness (out of the [players'] control both at deck building and at

> the table) should imply minimal impact.

I disagree. The proposition seems contrary to the philosophy of a
game that requires players to shuffle their decks. In any event, it
has no objective validity.

Moreover, your definition of "randomness", seems unduly restrictive
for current purposes. Any time a player is forced to cope with the
unknown and the unknowable (as when he makes a deck without knowing
what his opponents will play), outcomes are essentially "random" to
some extent from that players POV. And that seems the only relevant
issue when contrasting the impact of a player's luck versus his
skill. As in Rock Scissors Paper, there is no choice a player can
make that does not run the risk of being royally hosed by the choices
of his opponents.

If I accept your definition of "random", then contestation is not
random. It is merely the result of two players making the same
decision during deck contruction.

thing, the rule has no thematic value. For another, it has no effect

playgroup. For another, the rule is cumbersome, requiring 100 rolls

game.

hypothetical rule would be better if only the penalty were reduced
from 8 pool to (say) 1 pool. But I don't think this would make the
rule better. I think that, if anything, it would make it worse.
